accuracy.evidence: Checked against the DfE National Curriculum in England science (Year 2 living things and habitats and food chains; Year 4 food chains with predators and prey; Year 6 evolution and inheritance for the arms-race idea) and NGSS 3-LS4-3 and 4-LS1-1. Animal facts checked against National Geographic, Smithsonian's National Zoo and the Natural History Museum: grey wolves hunt elk and moose cooperatively; chameleon tongues are ballistic with a sticky tip and can exceed body length (Anderson 2016, Scientific Reports); many but not all spiders build webs; crocodiles ambush at the water's edge; porcupine quills, armadillo plates, skunk spray, poison dart frog toxins with aposematic colours and opossum thanatosis are documented defences; porcupines carry about 30,000 quills that regrow. Zebra stripes are deliberately left out because Caro et al. (2014, 2019) found the best-supported function is deterring biting flies, as the adult text explains. The arms-race model (slowest caught, survivors' young resemble them) follows Dawkins & Krebs (1979). Parameter answers w-y, g-c, f+a, k-p stay positive at every corner.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets documented children's ideas about adaptation and predation (Driver et al. 1994 'Making sense of secondary science', Bishop & Anderson 1990 on need-driven/Lamarckian change; Kampourakis & Zogza 2008 on teleological explanations): animals choose or try to change their bodies (prediction 'Each gazelle decides to grow faster legs', challenge tag chose, mastery m7), practice passed to offspring (tag practice), bright colours are for hiding (frog prediction, tag hide), every predator chases (crocodile chase option, tag chase), striking early (ambush 'Too soon' feedback), hunting together as laziness (tag lazy), the fastest prey being caught or capture being pure luck (catch-the-gazelle feedback, tags fast and luck), and one wolf being enough (pack step 'One wolf alone cannot stop a moose').

lab_distinct.evidence: flaghunt is built on predator–prey strategy: matching each hunter to its own trick, a timed crocodile ambush where striking outside the 'close' zone fails, dragging wolves into three escape gaps of a ring backed by a river so the hunt only succeeds when every gap is blocked, sorting prey by defence type, and a three-generation cheetah–gazelle race where removing the slowest raises the herd's average speed. It differs from flagchain and flagocfc (food chain order), flagcamo-style camouflage labs and flagmbmove (movement); the gate reports under 30% shingle overlap with every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each idea is discovered by doing: an early strike makes the gnu run, so waiting is shown to be the strategy; hunting with one or two wolves lets the moose escape through the open gap, so teamwork is shown to be necessary; the defence cards give the mechanism when placed; and picking the slowest gazelle three times visibly raises the average speed from 6.3 to 7.3 to 8.2, which the text then names as an arms race.

predictions.evidence: Five predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab disproves: chasing or web-building for the chameleon (the match step), 'It is asleep' or 'too slow' for the still crocodile (the ambush only works when it waits), 'Yes, easily' for one wolf against a moose (the moose escapes the gaps), 'So it can hide' for the bright frog (sorted as poison with a warning), and 'Each gazelle decides to grow faster legs' (the race shows selection, not choice). Task completion echoes the locked-in choice.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions with two wrong options each and a message per option: chase and trap (crocodiles ambush; spiders trap), lazy and web (teamwork catches big prey; webs are a spider trick), dead and armour (opossums play dead; armadillos have armour), hide and pretty (bright colours warn), fast and luck (the fastest escape; slow gazelles are caught more often), chose and practice (animals cannot choose their bodies; practice is not inherited). In-lab wrong moves also name the slip, e.g. 'Too soon! The gnu saw you and ran.'

readability.evidence: validate_lessons.py passes the learner limits; kid paragraphs use short sentences and define predator, prey, pack and ambush in plain words; adult text within 9.5. Canvas prompts are single instructions ('How does the wolf catch its food?', 'Drag wolves into the 3 gaps'). Precise terms for the age are used: predator, prey, pack, ambush, defence, quills, poisonous, generation, arms race.

no_filler.evidence: No filler pattern matches. Each step has one job (hunting tricks, ambush timing, teamwork, defences, selection over generations) and every feedback line gives the animal's mechanism or the reason a move failed. Item explanations give the reason rather than repeating the prompt.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360 px in light and dark, before and after Show me on every step. After the first pass the arms-race bars were tightened so the per-generation averages (gen 1: 6.3, gen 2: 7.3, gen 3: 8.2) sit above the feedback strip instead of under it. Trick tiles are two per row, the defence boxes three per row with wrapped labels, the wolf gaps have 26 px tap radius, and every canvas action is repeated by large buttons below the canvas.

accessibility.evidence: Everything is doable with buttons: the four trick buttons, 'Watch' and 'Strike!', 'Wolf to top/left/bottom gap' and 'Hunt', the three defence boxes, and one button per gazelle with its speed in the label. After each move the canvas aria-label states the scene, e.g. 'Catches: 1 of 2. The gnu is walking to the water.' or 'Generation 2. Speeds 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 9.'. The ambush gives the button user a 2.5-second window at the water's edge. Challenge feedback is an aria-live status. walk.cjs reports axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) clean in light and dark on desktop and iPhone 13 with no console errors.
